jurisdiction.name: San Diego
jurisdiction.notes: City of San Diego only; Chula Vista, Oceanside, Carlsbad, Escondido, Coronado and National City issue their own business and building permits. Health permits come from the County Department of Environmental Health and Quality, which requires a county-approved food handler card (the generic state card is not accepted).

permits.name: City of San Diego Business Tax Certificate
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Office of the City Treasurer
permits.notes: San Diego issues a Business Tax Certificate instead of a business license, and every business in the city needs one; apply online 24/7 and allow up to two weeks for the certificate. The annual tax is $34 for 12 or fewer employees or $125 plus $5 per employee for 13+, plus the $4 state SB 1186 fee and a $1.47-per-employee minimum wage enforcement fee (Business Improvement District assessments may be added). Pay within 15 days of your start date to avoid a $25-or-10% late fee; you must also self-certify that the use is allowed by zoning.

permits.name: Fictitious Business Name (DBA) statement – San Diego County
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego County Assessor/Recorder/County Clerk
permits.notes: File within 40 days of first transacting business under a name other than your legal name. The filing fee is $54 for the first business name and registrant (card payments add a $2.50 surcharge); within 45 days you must publish the notice in a newspaper of general circulation for four consecutive weeks. Banks, ABC and the business tax application expect the filed statement.

permits.name: Food Establishment Wastewater Discharge (FEWD) permit and grease plan check
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Public Utilities Department – FEWD Program
permits.notes: Every food service establishment in the City needs a FEWD permit, and all new, remodeled or retrofitted food facilities must get a FEWD plan review of their grease-removal equipment; plan review is currently free (call 858-654-4188). High-volume and new restaurants are typically required to install an outdoor gravity grease interceptor with a sample box rather than an under-sink hydromechanical unit. County DEH expects FEWD approval before you submit food plan check documents for a City of San Diego location.
permits.stall_risk: Being told late that you need an exterior gravity interceptor (with excavation, a sample box and three manholes) can add weeks and five figures to a build-out. Get the FEWD sizing decision before the County plan check and building permit drawings are finalized.

permits.name: Food facility plan check (new construction / remodel)
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego County Dept. of Environmental Health and Quality – Food and Housing Division, Plan Check
permits.notes: New food facilities, tenant improvements, remodels and equipment changes need DEH plan approval before construction. Submit the application, fee, plans, menu, equipment cut sheets and finish samples; DEH approves or rejects within 20 working days. FY2026–27 fees run $1,534 (up to 1,999 sq ft) to $3,407 (10,000+ sq ft), minor remodels $670, and each resubmittal after corrections costs $1,087, followed by required mid-construction (50–80%) and final inspections.
permits.stall_risk: Each correction round costs a $1,087 resubmittal fee plus another review cycle, and skipping the required 50–80% mid-construction inspection can force walls to be reopened. Use the DEH submission checklist and book the mid-construction inspection on schedule.

permits.name: Health permit to operate a food facility
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego County Dept. of Environmental Health and Quality – Food and Housing Division
permits.notes: Issued by plan check staff after the final inspection confirms the facility matches approved plans, a certified food safety manager is on staff and every food handler has a San Diego County food handler card. FY2026–27 annual restaurant permits are tiered by employees: $842 (1–10), $987 (11–25), $1,170 (26–100) and $2,087 (101+), plus $649 for each food-prep area beyond three. A change of ownership requires a new application.
permits.stall_risk: Final inspections fail on missing food handler cards as often as on construction items, because the state card is not accepted in San Diego County. Have every staff member hold a county-approved card before the final.

permits.name: San Diego County food handler card (county program – state card not accepted)
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego County Dept. of Environmental Health and Quality via county-authorized training schools
permits.notes: San Diego County Code requires every food handler to hold either a card from a county-authorized food handler school or a pass on the County food handler test given by the facility's certified food safety manager ($2 training packet from DEH). Not every California (ANSI) course is approved for San Diego County, so a generic state food handler card does not satisfy inspectors here. Cards last three years and renewal requires a 3-hour course and test.

permits.name: Building permit (tenant improvements / change of use)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department (DSD)
permits.notes: Kitchen build-outs, hoods, restrooms, ADA work and any change of occupancy need a DSD building permit with plans by a licensed designer. Simple projects can use Rapid Review (formerly over-the-counter) at no extra cost; Express plan check costs an admin fee plus 1.5x the regular plan check fee. Plan review, inspection, water/sewer capacity and development impact fees vary by project (Information Bulletin 501), and historic review applies to buildings 45+ years old.
permits.stall_risk: Change-of-occupancy projects often trigger sewer/water capacity fees, accessibility upgrades and historic review that were not in the budget. Request a DSD preliminary review before signing the lease.

permits.name: Certificate of Occupancy (change of use / new building)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department (DSD)
permits.notes: DSD issues a Certificate of Occupancy after final building inspection when a building is new or changes occupancy group (e.g. retail to an A-2 restaurant or bar). The posted occupant load on the certificate is what SDPD asks for as evidence of maximum occupancy on live entertainment applications. Plan the final inspection sequence so fire, building and DEH finals land in the same week.

permits.name: Fire permit – kitchen hood suppression, fire alarm and sprinklers
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department (fire plan review) / San Diego Fire-Rescue Department
permits.notes: Installing or modifying a kitchen hood suppression system, fire alarm or sprinklers requires a DSD fire permit; under Information Bulletin 506 a hood suppression system costs $264.25 for plan review plus $353.13 for inspection, with alarms and sprinklers priced by device count. Assembly occupancies (50+ occupants) also need occupancy classification and posted occupant load from DSD, and SDFD Fire Prevention conducts the fire inspections. Book the hood and alarm finals before the DEH final inspection.

permits.name: Zoning Use Verification for an ABC license (ABC-255)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department
permits.notes: Every ABC license application in the City of San Diego needs a Zoning Use Verification: submit the ABC-255 form online as a miscellaneous application and pay the $706.27 Alcoholic Beverage Review Fee plus $12.16 mapping fee. Most on-sale restaurants and bars are confirmed administratively here; off-sale outlets (Type 20/21) face extra distance and concentration limits under SDMC §141.0502. ABC will not complete your license without the City's zoning sign-off.

permits.name: Conditional Use Permit (nightclub / off-sale alcohol outlet)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department – Hearing Officer / Planning Commission
permits.notes: A discretionary Conditional Use Permit (Process Three, decided by a Hearing Officer after a public hearing) is needed for uses the zone only allows conditionally, such as nightclubs and dance venues in many zones and off-sale alcohol outlets that fail the SDMC §141.0502 location limits. Information Bulletin 503 requires an $8,000 initial deposit plus about $1,277 in administrative fees, drawn down by staff time, plus CEQA review and an appeal period. Most sit-down restaurants and neighborhood bars do not need one; confirm with a DSD preliminary review.
permits.stall_risk: Hearing scheduling, community planning group review and appeals typically take 6–12 months, and a deposit account can run well past the initial $8,000. Keep the lease contingent on the CUP and engage the community planning group early.

permits.name: Public Convenience or Necessity (PCN) finding for a bar license
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego Police Department (applications through the Office of the City Treasurer)
permits.notes: ABC Type 40, 42 and 48 (bar) licenses in census tracts that are over-concentrated with licenses or have crime above 120% of the city average need a PCN investigation by SDPD; restaurant licenses (Types 41/47) are not on the list. Get the ABC-245 form showing your tract's concentration and crime figures, then pay $2,728 at the City Treasurer; SDPD has 90 days to investigate and replies by certified letter, with 10 days to appeal a denial. Only applies if ABC says your tract triggers it.
permits.stall_risk: SDPD can take the full 90 days and may deny in high-crime downtown or beach tracts, which stops the ABC transfer. Ask ABC for the tract figures before signing the lease and prepare a security and operations plan for the investigation.

permits.name: Police permit for live entertainment (ongoing)
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego Police Department – Permits and Licensing (processed by the Office of the City Treasurer)
permits.notes: Businesses with ongoing live entertainment (music, DJs, dancing, performances) are police-regulated under SDMC Chapter 3, Article 3 and need an annual SDPD permit; SDPD runs a 30-day background investigation once the complete packet is filed in person at the City Treasurer. Annual regulatory fees: $262 (no alcohol or dancing, 49 or fewer people) or $1,207 (50+); with alcohol or dancing, $2,369 (99 or fewer) up to $6,230 (400+), plus the $87 new-application fee and $24 per additional owner. You need zoning approval, evidence of maximum occupancy and any required CUP first.

permits.name: Police permit for after-hours entertainment (2 am – 6 am)
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego Police Department – Permits and Licensing (processed by the Office of the City Treasurer)
permits.notes: Venues offering entertainment between 2 am and 6 am need a separate after-hours police permit: $1,055 per year for ongoing operation (or $832 per one-time event) plus the $87 application fee. Alcohol service must still end at 2 am under state law, and SDPD conditions typically cover security staffing and dispersal. File it with the ongoing live entertainment permit so both background checks run together.

permits.name: Sign permit (exterior business signage)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department
permits.notes: Most new or replaced exterior signs need a DSD sign permit with a sign plan and sign schedule (Information Bulletin 111); small non-illuminated nameplates and warning signs are exempt. Monument signs over 7 feet, structural signs and historic sites may also need a building permit or historic review. Inspection and review fees vary by sign type.

permits.name: Spaces as Places outdoor dining permit (sidewalk café / streetary)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department – Public Right-of-Way Permit
permits.notes: Ordinance O-21391 permanently allows sidewalk cafés, streetaries and active sidewalks in the public right-of-way through a Public Right-of-Way Permit (Process One) valid for two years; asking for deviations from code turns it into a Process Two Neighborhood Use Permit ($19,962 flat fee for a sidewalk café NUP). For a one-space streetary the City estimates about $6,500 in permitting and inspection plus a two-year exclusive-use fee of $4,427–$13,283 depending on the area. You need an active business tax certificate, $1M/$2M general liability plus a $4M umbrella naming the City, and an encroachment maintenance and removal agreement; grants of up to $20,000 are available.

permits.name: Transient Occupancy Registration Certificate (TOT / TMD)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Office of the City Treasurer
permits.notes: Any property renting rooms to transients (stays under one month) needs a Transient Occupancy Registration Certificate before collecting TOT; apply by emailing the application to sdtot@sandiego.gov. Since May 1, 2025 (Measure C) the city has three TOT zones at 11.75%, 12.75% and 13.75%, and lodging businesses with 70+ rooms also pay the Tourism Marketing District assessment. TOT is collected with rent, held in trust and remitted monthly.

permits.name: Mobile Food Facility health permit and plan review (truck / cart)
permits.issuing_agency: San Diego County Dept. of Environmental Health and Quality – Food and Housing Division
permits.notes: Trucks and carts need a DEH plan review ($293 prepackaged / $545 open food prep in FY2026–27) and an annual mobile food facility permit ($228–$760 depending on type), tied to an approved commissary with a signed commissary letter. Out-of-county commissaries need a separate letter. Staff must also hold San Diego County food handler cards.

permits.name: Mobile Food Truck Permit (private property locations)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department
permits.notes: Required to operate a food truck on private property (lots, breweries, office parks); on-street operation is exempt but trucks are barred from the right-of-way in the Parking Impact Overlay Zone and from daily operation in the Gaslamp Quarter. Information Bulletin 148 lists annual fees of $737 (General Plan Maintenance) + $706.27 plan check + $12.16 mapping. Trucks may not sell or serve alcohol.

permits.name: Sidewalk Vending Permit (carts and stands)
permits.issuing_agency: City of San Diego Office of the City Treasurer
permits.notes: Roaming or stationary vendors selling from pushcarts, wagons or stands on sidewalks or public property need a Sidewalk Vending Permit (valid one year), a Business Tax Certificate and a City photo ID, applied for in person by appointment (TRSPDPermits@sandiego.gov, 619-615-1500). Bring your seller's permit, government ID and, for food, the County health permit and food handler card. Check the City's sidewalk vending maps for prohibited zones such as beaches, parks and areas near events.
